title: Discussion: Is the 2026 Detroit Lions defense fixable?
summary: If it weren’t for Ford Field being indoors, you could easily see the sky falling on the Detroit Lions. Although the team sits at 2-2 on the season, things feel far more grim. The Lions defensive ineptitudes once again stole the spotlight for the wrong reasons. Because the defense is struggling to stop any opponent, […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard walks off the field after 32-26 loss to Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co If it weren’t for Ford Field being indoors, you could easily see the sky falling on the Detroit Lions. Although the team sits at 2-2 on the season, things feel far more grim. The Lions defensive ineptitudes once again stole the spotlight for the wrong reasons. Because the defense is struggling to stop any opponent, it is leading to the offense having to muster a perfect game. The Lions managed to stay alive against the New Orleans Saints in Week 1 and the New York Jets in Week 3, but things came crashing down against the Carolina Panthers. The Lions offense has some issues to work through, but not only is there a blueprint for success there, we have seen enough flashes through four weeks to instill some faith and confidence. The same cannot be said about the defense, a unit that has sunk the Lions early in the season. The question going forward is whether the Lions can bail their way out of this shipwreck, or if the defense will continue to drag them to the depths of the NFL. Today’s Question of the Day is: Is the 2026 Detroit Lions defense fixable? My answer: No. I want to be optimistic about the defense—I really do. Aidan Hutchinson is making an impact on every snap. Alim McNeill has rebounded phenomenally in 2026 and looks like the player that deserved a $97 million contract. Jack Campbell is coming off an All-Pro season. Tyleik Williams has taken a big step in his second season. D.J. Wonnum has been a solid addition to the defensive line. Derrick Barnes looks much-improved after a rough 2025 campaign. Brian Branch is seemingly close to returning . For all the faults in the secondary, the defense has enough pieces that it should at least look competent. We are not asking for the prime Baltimore Ravens or Seattle Seahawks that led their team to a Super Bowl. This Lions team could suffice with even an average or below-average defense. Instead, we are facing one of the worst starts to a season in history: Most points per game allowed in a season in the last 40 years: 2020 Lions – 32.4 2008 Lions – 32.3 2026 Lions – 31.8 (through 4 games) — NFL Researcher (@NFL_Researcher) October 5, 2026 The 2020 Lions team went 5-11 and was the dying corpse of the Matt Patricia era. The 2008 team was the infamous 0-16 team in contention for worst team in history. The fact that the 2026 Lions are meant to be in their Super Bowl window and are trotting out a defense like this is inexcusable. Worse yet, I think that the Lions have made their bed with the 2026 roster. They will live and likely die by their defense playing incapable football. No amount of in-season adjustments can fix it. I do not think that firing Kelvin Sheppard will solve the issue. Whether his replacement came from inside or outside the organization, the team would have to undergo a significant identity change within the span of a few weeks. This is something that can happen over the course of a training camp. I do not see this happening midseason, especially with an early Week 6 bye. One argument in favor of firing Sheppard is justifiable: it’s not like the Lions can get much worse, right? For how chaotic a midseason schematic change could be, the Lions clearly cannot continue with the status quo . However, I think too many things would have to go right to course correct the defense. At this point, there is no singular solution. Unfortunately, the Lions simply do not have time to correct most of their mistakes. Let us examine a best-case scenario. Not only do the Lions need Brian Branch to return to the lineup soon, but they would also need him to return at a high level—looking at McNeill’s 2025 campaign, you can see how that is far from guarantee. Perhaps even Kerby Joseph returns, although it presently feels like Santa Claus could return before Joseph. If the Lions do make a coaching change, that coordinator would have to overhaul a playbook months in the making in a matter of weeks, all while improving communication and execution. Finally, the Lions would have to add more talent to the secondary via trade, moves that would surely cost them capital and cap space and threaten their ability to restock in 2027—something that might be necessary at this rate. On top of all that, the Lions need the current roster to stay healthy. I am not trying to have a knee-jerk reaction, but four games is enough of a sample size to be concerned. For the Lions to turn around this defense, they need a lot to go in their favor.
author: John Whiticar

title: The Packers need to clean up their penalties problem
summary: NFL officiating has jumped the shark this season. Not only are officials throwing more flags than ever, but they are also throwing them more in the biggest moments of the game. After two officials crossed the line this week and were unprofessional toward players, the league finally cracked down on the stripes and suspended a […]
full_text: (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images NFL officiating has jumped the shark this season. Not only are officials throwing more flags than ever , but they are also throwing them more in the biggest moments of the game . After two officials crossed the line this week and were unprofessional toward players , the league finally cracked down on the stripes and suspended a line judge for multiple games and a referee for one. League-wide, there’s a push and pull with officials, but in the Green Bay Packers’ case, not all of their woes can be explained by that. Yes, the Packers are getting flagged more this year. Yes, NFL games are getting penalized more. No, the Packers are not keeping regular pace with the rest of the league. Your eyes aren’t lying to you; the Packers are getting flagged at a high rate, even during this flag inflation. This post isn’t to complain about officiating, but rather to explain how Green Bay is losing “hidden yardage” this year. I don’t blame the refs for all of the Packers’ calls this year (though that one drive against Minnesota is still nuts to think about). This is a sloppy operation, particularly on the offensive side of the ball. With that being said, I think the offense took a pretty good step forward last week — outside of penalties and ball security. If they can just clean that up, Green Bay could be off to the races and back in the playoff conversation. As of now, the Packers have racked up 36 flags on the road (12 per game) compared to just 6 at home for their lone home game. Those 36 road flags lead the NFL, with the Arizona Cardinals — coached by Green Bay head coach Matt LaFleur’s younger brother — coming in second place with 25. On the road, when the offense has to operate in a silent count due to noise, the Packers’ offense is not playing cleanly. Through four weeks, Green Bay ranks second in total penalties, third in total pre-snap penalties and third in net penalties. If you want to throw out Week 1 as a weird mulligan week for everyone in the sport, the Packers have still posted 18 offensive penalties (compared to just seven on defense and five on special teams). Maybe most importantly, though, the Green Bay offense is hurting themselves on first downs, which impacts the entire offensive series, far too often. So far in 2026, the Packers have been flagged 15 times on offense on first downs, the most in the league — with 13 of those coming in the last three weeks. More than half of those (eight) came on holding calls, with four false starts being the other category where the Packers received multiple infractions. To get the train back on the tracks, Green Bay is going to have to eliminate their 1st-and-20 and 1st-and-15 looks on offense. It’s hurting them consistently this year. It’s easier to point at a problem than to solve it, as I’m sure the Packers’ players have been instructed not to draw flags, but the team has to find a way to overcome their offensive penalties on the road. The offense’s penalty pace in road games, particularly on first downs, just cannot continue.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Packers Discussion: How are you feeling about the team after Week 4?
summary: I figured we should open up a discussion about where the Green Bay Packers are, since this seems like an important snapshot of the team before they end up playing the Chicago Bears in Week 5. I just got through the offense’s film from Week 4, and here are my general thoughts: 1) Jordan Love […]
full_text: (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images I figured we should open up a discussion about where the Green Bay Packers are, since this seems like an important snapshot of the team before they end up playing the Chicago Bears in Week 5. I just got through the offense’s film from Week 4, and here are my general thoughts: 1) Jordan Love played much better than in the previous two weeks, mostly because he looked calm in the pocket. Really, his nerves started to show up in the fourth quarter of Week 1, when it seemed like he lost all trust in the offensive line. He was moving in pockets that he just didn’t trust anymore (and I don’t really blame him). This week, that all went away. Marshawn Lloyd with the early candidate for Hurdle of the Year! Turns out he was encouraged by a Packers coach to go over the top, after the Bucs went low and forced Lloyd to fumble on the drive before. pic.twitter.com/ABa8lRxkQT — Pat Timlin (@pat_timlin) October 5, 2026 I think the best example of this is the play where MarShawn Lloyd hurdled a Buccaneers defender. Love is operating a quick-game pass (the ball is supposed to be out fast), but he was comfortable enough with the line blocking an extra second or two to find his checkdown. In previous weeks, he probably would have moved around and just hoped for a scramble drill. The only bad balls I saw were the deep shot to J. Michael Sturdivant (he only played one more snap after it looked like he slowed down instead of running through the route — potentially the fault of Sturdivant and not Love) and the deep shot to Matthew Golden. I don’t even really put the interception on Love, since the deep thirds defender just broke his rules on the play and left Jonnu Smith wide open. The entire game plan was about reading the defense quickly and throwing the ball quickly, so a defender going off script got him (sort of like the interception late against the Cleveland Browns last year). 2) They can run an offense now! They did enough in the run game to have the defense respect the run on play-action reps, arguably the biggest benefit to running the ball. Was it always pretty? No! The backs mostly went down on first contact, even against cornerbacks in duo schemes (the reason you run these plays is to get the backs one-on-one with cornerbacks), but they did enough to make play-action plays relevant — something that wasn’t true last week against the Atlanta Falcons. On the 4th and 1 at the goal line Rhyan blows a block and the DT doesn't even think about playing the run, goes straight to Jordan. If DL aren't thinking run in short yardage at the goal line, you're fucked beyond belief. Get Monk off the field and run gap so you can do anything https://t.co/p3QUVC1xMv pic.twitter.com/SU7lPIXbwX — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 25, 2026 This was probably the first time since Week 1 (when the Packers were a full-blown outside zone and boot action offense, a poor one at that) that the running game complemented the passing game. I’m counting that as progress! 3) We’re making the lives of our offensive linemen easier with the quick passing game and screen game. The Packers aren’t getting a ton of YAC out of these plays (Tucker Kraft doesn’t look 100 percent right now), but it’s at least moving the chains pretty regularly. I don’t know how good this offensive line will look from a pass protection standpoint if the game gets out of hand and they’re chasing points, but at least when they’re on schedule, they can survive with what they’re doing right now. Staying on schedule is going to be huge for this team, as quick-game passes, screens and play-action passes sort of rely on the opposing defense not assuming a pass is coming every single play. We’re going to learn a lot about this line the next time they’re actually chasing points. 4) Way too many penalties. Way too many drops. Stupid fumbles (including the one that thankfully was ruled a drop for Matthew Golden). If the Packers can just fix that, things will look a lot better on offense, even if their running backs aren’t breaking tackles and the team isn’t getting breakaway YAC performances from checkdowns. — There’s plenty of work to be done, but this week was a step in a positive direction, in some aspects — like the gameplan and the function of the offensive line. Other areas — like shooting themselves in the foot with penalties, drops and fumbles — still need improvement. Let me know what you think of the team in the comments section. When I watch the defense, I’ll add some of my thoughts there, too. Join the conversation! title: Packers’ Matt LaFleur gives injury updates on Brandon Cisse, Chris Brooks and Micah Parsons
summary: Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur spoke at length about the Packers’ injuries sustained during Week 4 in his Monday press conference. According to LaFleur, the team will attempt to replace linebacker Edgerrin Cooper, who is out for the year with a ruptured Achilles, with some combination of Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper — […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur spoke at length about the Packers’ injuries sustained during Week 4 in his Monday press conference. According to LaFleur, the team will attempt to replace linebacker Edgerrin Cooper, who is out for the year with a ruptured Achilles, with some combination of Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper — not a shocking revelation, since that’s what we saw on Sunday. Beyond Cooper, LaFleur stated that cornerback Brandon Cisse is not in the concussion protocol and that his neck injury is not “anything long-term.” Cisse dropped out against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers with a neck injury and was being evaluated for a concussion. Carrington Valentine replaced him at right cornerback on Sunday. Running back Chris Brooks, who was out-snapping all other Packers running backs through four weeks before his injury against Tampa, is still having his ankle evaluated, so his status is pretty open-ended. If Green Bay is out Brooks, look for Green Bay to elevate running back Pierre Strong Jr. from the practice squad — potentially with the 53-man roster spot that Cooper has now opened up. On the topic of edge defender Micah Parsons, LaFleur said that Parsons will not practice this week but that the All-Pro is doing his best to get back on the field quickly. LaFleur claimed that Parsons made up ground in the last week or so, but that “where and when he’ll be available, time will tell.” There were no updates on the four other players on the Packers’ IR-designated to return list or their physically unable to perform list: receiver Savion Williams (IR-DFR), tight end Luke Musgrave (PUP), defensive lineman Jordon Riley (PUP) and edge rusher Collin Oliver (IR-DFR). Like Parsons, these players were all first eligible to return to practice in Week 3, with a full return available starting in Week 5, based on the NFL’s rules.

title: The Packers’ easy portion of the schedule is over
summary: According to ESPN’s Football Power Index, which has now been updated for Week 4’s action, the Green Bay Packers have played the 31st schedule in the NFL through four games — the second-easiest schedule in the league so far, only behind the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs. Moving forward, they’ll have the second-hardest schedule in the […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to ESPN’s Football Power Index , which has now been updated for Week 4’s action, the Green Bay Packers have played the 31st schedule in the NFL through four games — the second-easiest schedule in the league so far, only behind the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs. Moving forward, they’ll have the second-hardest schedule in the league from Weeks 5 to 18 — per FPI. Here is how ESPN explains FPI: The Football Power Index (FPI) is a measure of team strength that is meant to be the best predictor of a team’s performance going forward for the rest of the season. FPI represents how many points above or below average a team is. Projected results are based on 10,000 simulations of the rest of the season using FPI, results to date, and the remaining schedule. Ratings and projections update daily. Below are the games the Packers have played so far: Week 1: @ MIN (4-0) Week 2: @ NYJ (1-3) Week 3: vs. ATL (1-2) Week 4: @ TB (0-4) The only team with a winning record that they’ve played so far is Minnesota, the first NFL team to start 4-0 without scoring a touchdown in two of those games since the 1934 Detroit Lions. (With that being said, I do think the Jets are a little underrated , and there was a noticeable difference for the Falcons when Michael Penix Jr. was under center for the team.) Moving forward, here is the Packers’ schedule: Week 5: vs. CHI (3-1) Week 6: vs. DAL (2-2) Week 7: @ DET (2-2) Week 8: vs. CAR (2-2) Week 9: @ NE (2-2) Week 10: vs. MIN (4-0) Week 11: BYE week Week 12: @ LAR (2-2) Week 13: @ NO (1-2) Week 14: vs. BUF (3-1) Week 15: vs. MIA (0-4) Week 16: @ CHI (3-1) Week 17: vs. HOU (0-4) Week 18: vs. DET (2-2) The only sub-.500 teams left on the Packers’ schedule right now are the Saints in Week 13 (New Orleans hasn’t played in Week 4, and could be 2-2 by the end of Monday’s action), the Dolphins in Week 14 and the Texans in Week 17. For perspective, 0-4 Houston has been able to keep games closer this year, as they have a -25 point differential compared to the 2-2 Packers’ -32 point differential. The Saints only have a -2 point differential, despite being 1-2. The only team left on Green Bay’s schedule with a worse point differential than the Packers is the 0-4 Dolphins, who have by far the worst mark in the league at -55. We all knew the Packers got a good break to start the season coming in, considering their injury situation. What we didn’t fully see was the team going just 2-2 to start the year and suffering four season-ending injuries in the first four weeks of 2026. Green Bay needs to buckle down for the rest of the regular season, as the schedule difficulty is only going to get tougher.

title: Travis Glover passes the test in first significant playing time since 2024
summary: After upending their offensive line over the post-Thursday Night Football mini bye, the Packers coaching staff reached into a hat and pulled out a new name to start at right guard for Sunday’s game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Instead of Kevin Zeitler or Donovan Jennings or Jacob Monk or Jager Burton, it was Travis […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - AUGUST 18: Travis Glover #79 of the Green Bay Packers steps up to block during an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on August 18, 2024 in Denver, CO. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images After upending their offensive line over the post-Thursday Night Football mini bye, the Packers coaching staff reached into a hat and pulled out a new name to start at right guard for Sunday’s game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Instead of Kevin Zeitler or Donovan Jennings or Jacob Monk or Jager Burton, it was Travis Glover getting the nod between Sean Rhyan and Anthony Belton. A 2024 sixth round pick, we haven’t seen Glover on the field for a game that matters in quite some time. The last time he made an appearance was in the Packers’ loss to the eventual Super Bowl champion Philadelphia Eagles, when he came in at left guard in relief of an injured Elgton Jenkins, who dropped out after just four plays. Facing off against a ferocious Philadelphia front, Glover was penalized three times before he was ultimately benched in favor of Kadeem Telfort. However, after an injury to starting center Josh Myers forced Sean Rhyan to take over at center, Glover got back into the game at right guard. All told, he played 33 snaps and had a dreadful day, posting a pass blocking grade of just 1.8 according to Pro Football Focus. For comparison, Donovan Jennings and Jacob Monk put up pass blocking grades of 40.0 and 48.2, respectively, in the Packers’ Week 1 loss to the Vikings this season, and that was one of the single-worst blocking performances we’ve ever seen. You can and should take PFF grades with a grain of salt, but that’s a startling difference. Glover missed all of the 2025 season with a back injury, but was back in action this preseason lining up primarily but not exclusively at right tackle. He played 39 snaps on the outside against just 28 at right guard, but with Jennings struggling, Monk unavailable due to injury, and Burton’s NFL experience coming primarily at left guard, those 28 snaps apparently represented enough time on task to give Glover the start. How did Glover do? It wasn’t a spectacular day for the Packers on the ground or through the air, but Glover came close to achieving a lineman’s ideal day: by and large, he was seen but not heard. In 60 snaps of work, he surrendered just one pressure and was penalized one time, a holding penalty on the Packers’ first offensive play of the fourth quarter. A 19-yard completion to Jonnu Smith on the next play erased that penalty and then some, though, so ultimately it was of little consequence. Pro Football Focus gave Glover a 59.4 grade overall, bolstered mainly by his 71.4 grade as a pass blocker (they gave him a 53.8 grade for his run blocking). That aligns well with the eye test of the Packers’ offensive line as a whole; by and large, they did a good job protecting Jordan Love but struggled to get much push in the ground game. It wasn’t necessarily Glover’s fault, but you can see some of the struggles the Packers had on the ground in a 2nd and 3 play in the second quarter. Jordan Morgan gives up ground to Buccaneers’ defensive lineman Rakeem Nunez-Roches so quickly that Glover, coming right to left as a pulling guard, ends up smacking Morgan in the face. For a second, it looks like Glover and Morgan are giving each other a hug as Nunez-Roches takes Kaleb Johnson down for a two-yard loss. But in a game where the Packers’ offensive line looked relatively competent, especially compared to the rest of the season, Glover, at the very least, was not obviously bad. That’s a step in the right direction. And hopefully, it’ll be the last the Packers see of him for a while. It was probably unrealistic to expect newly arrived Kevin Zeitler in the lineup this week, but going forward, he’ll hopefully be ready to go. Whatever workouts he’s been doing on his own were almost assuredly not enough to get him from “active, but sitting at home” to “ready to play in an NFL game” in roughly three days of practice, one of which would have been at walkthrough speed. He was always going to need some time, and hopefully another week will do it. But if he can’t go, the Packers should at least feel good putting Glover out there again. He wasn’t a clear detriment to the team’s performance, and given what we’ve seen from his teammates this year, that’s a huge compliment.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: NFL officials are calling more penalties than ever
summary: If you’ve been feeling like NFL football fields have been awash in yellow this season, your eyes have not deceived you. NFL officials are calling more penalties per game than they have in any season dating back to 2009, and it’s not particularly close. According to data from NFLPenalties.com, NFL officials are calling a little […]
full_text: OAKLAND, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 08: A yellow penalty flag lays on the field during the second half of the game between the Oakland Raiders and the Tennessee Titans at RingCentral Coliseum on December 08, 2019 in Oakland, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you’ve been feeling like NFL football fields have been awash in yellow this season, your eyes have not deceived you. NFL officials are calling more penalties per game than they have in any season dating back to 2009, and it’s not particularly close. According to data from NFLPenalties.com , NFL officials are calling a little more than 17 penalties per game this season, the most we’ve seen in any single year since 2009. The average game includes 15 accepted penalties, also the most we’ve seen in any single year in that same time span. The previous highs in both of those categories are 16.2 total flags per game and 13.7 accepted penalties per game, both of which happened in 2015. The Packers, as you no doubt are aware, are one of the hardest hit teams in this ongoing festival of penalties, averaging 10.5 penalties per game. And for those inclined to say this is a long-term issue for Matt LaFleur’s teams, it really isn’t. Outside of this year, LaFleur’s Packers have typically been right in line with the league average for individual team penalties per game; they’ve never averaged more than 6.2 accepted penalties per game in any season since 2019. In short, NFL games have been flag fests. What’s causing the increase? There are a few specific penalties to blame, but it’s all on the offense’s shoulders. Offensive holding, false start, and delay of game have all seen the biggest increases in per game calls from 2025 to 2026. Holding is being called, on average, 3.13 times per game leaguewide, up from 2.4 per game last year. We’re seeing 2.78 false start flags per game this year, up from 2.39 last year. And to round things out, we’ve seen an average of 0.97 delay of game penalties per week, an increase from 0.64 last year. Those penalties alone don’t account for the increase, though it comes pretty close. But in general, NFL games are seeing more and more penalties; across the 49 different infractions already called at least once this year, 26 are being called at a higher rate than last year. Just 15 are being called at a lower rate. Generally speaking, if you’re tuning in to watch NFL football this season, chances are good you’re going to see more penalties than ever before.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Packers Film Room: Long snapping on kicks in Week 4
summary: In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We only have 3 that we’re looking at this week, so it’ll probably be a quick one. No blocked field goals to break down like we did last week. As we always do, we’ll start with the snap location for […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 28: Long snapper Matt Orzech #42 of the Green Bay Packers warms up prior to an NFL game against the Miami Dolphins at Lambeau Field on November 28, 2024 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We only have 3 that we’re looking at this week, so it’ll probably be a quick one. No blocked field goals to break down like we did last week . As we always do, we’ll start with the snap location for the holder. How did it look this week? The exact same as last week in terms of breakdown. Two up and into the body, one over the hold spot. Let’s look at the individual kicks, with the snap-to-hold operation slowed down to 30% speed. Kick 1: Extra Point (Made) Snap up and to the body of Whelan. Clean catch and hold. No wind and extra point distance, so we get a slight lean forward and away from the kicker on the hold. It’s worth noting that the block last week was a result of Donovan Jennings being late out of his stance. Travis Glover is in that spot this week, and he is able to make himself big and not allow pressure from his outside shoulder. One other thing to keep an eye on: Karl Brooks is the outside man on the left side of your screen. He’s slightly late to react to the snap and doesn’t force Zyon McCollum [27] wide, which allows McCollum to bend the edge and almost get a hand on the ball. Kick 2: 58 Yard Field Goal (Made) Great snap. Up and over the hold spot (slightly into the body, but I’m counting it as over the hold spot). With the distance of the kick, the lean on the hold is slightly more forward than we saw on the extra point. Brooks is on the right side of the screen. Once more McCollum is looking to bend the edge, but Brooks gets a hand on him and is able to disrupt him just enough. Good snap. Good hold. Booming kick from Smack. Kick 3: Extra Point (Made) Good snap, up and into the body. Good hold by Whelan. Smack splits the uprights. Once again, McCollum is on the edge vs Brooks (right side of the screen). Brooks has seen this movie before. With Belton slowing down the gap between him and Brooks, Brooks turns and gives McCollum a nice knock, sending him to the turf. Albums listened to: Nine Inch Nails – Ghosts V: Together
author: Dusty Evely

title: Packers By The Numbers: Stats from the Week 4 win over the Bucs
summary: As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers game, courtesy of SumerSports. Offense Last week saw the Packers needing to lean heavy into 11 personnel and the passing game, due to getting behind early and also lacking any ability to run. This week saw them […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 4: Xavier McKinney #29 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates a sack against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the game at Raymond James Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers game, courtesy of SumerSports . Offense Last week saw the Packers needing to lean heavy into 11 personnel and the passing game, due to getting behind early and also lacking any ability to run. This week saw them with a little more balance, both in terms of personnel usage and in run/pass ratio. This week, the Packers were in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) on just 47.3% of their snaps (down from 81% last week). They were in 12 personnel on 23.6% and 13 personnel on 29.1% of their snaps. That 13 personnel rate (1 RB, 3 TE, 1 WR) was their highest usage of that personnel package this year, and it was also their best passing package. When operating out of 13 personnel, Jordan Love was 5/5 for 76 yards for an EPA per Play of +1.04 (basically, they generated a little more than 1 point every time they passed out of this grouping). They had a 100% Success Rate when passing out of 13 personnel. It was also their best running group (11 attempts, 52 yards, -0.09 EPA per Play). I’m excited to dig into the film on that and see what they were doing when in that personnel group. On the run/pass ratio, the Packers passed 56.4% of the time and ran 43.6% of the time. That’s a far cry from the 85.7% pass rate we saw against the Falcons. The pass game (+0.14 EPA per Play) far outperformed the run game (-0.35). While an 85.7% pass rate is a bit extreme, I’d certainly like to see the pass rate be a little closer to 65% rather than 55%. Love was still getting the ball out quickly (he averaged 2.17 seconds to throw, a full 0.5 seconds below the NFL average), with an EPA per Play of +0.14. That’s far and away his best passing performance of the year. Before this, his best performance was in the Vikings game in Week 1, where he posted an EPA per Play of -0.02. For the first time this year, Love took 0 sacks. There were some plays he’d like to have back and there were (once again) a couple drops, but this is the most competent the Packers offense has looked all year. Love also looked good against the blitz. That’s been an issue all year (mainly because, against the line through the first 3 weeks, a blitz meant an automatic pressure), but Love did well this week. Against the blitz, he was 7/9 for 62 yards (+0.14 EPA per Play). It was also an encouraging performance from Tucker Kraft. He caught 6 of his 7 targets for 42 yards and a TD, good for +0.79 EPA per Reception. He had an ADOT (Average Depth of Target) of 0.57 yards and he averaged 6.83 yards after the catch. He wasn’t asked to stretch the field very much (his targets were on Hitches and Quick Outs), but when he got the ball in his hands he got upfield and was looking to make something happen. He still doesn’t look like the Tucker Kraft we were used to seeing last season, but this was the first time all year we really got a good glimpse of that guy. Overall, Kraft had a 22.6% target share. He was a heavy target in the Red Zone (42.9% target share) and saw a decent amount of looks on early downs (27.3% early down target share). Kraft also had an EPA per Play of +1.93 on rush attempts, thanks to his successful 4th down sneak. Here’s what the running game numbers looked like from Gap Outcomes, by running back. Chris Brooks: Kaleb Johnson: MarShawn Lloyd: Brooks is their most limited runner in terms of burst/wiggle, but, if the line can block it up, he’s been their most effective because he can read his blocks and hit the hole. Let’s take a quick look at the guards before moving to the other side of the ball. Last week, Jacob Monk (LG) allowed 8.3% pressure rate, with a 22.2% pressure rate against blitz, 5.3% pressure rate vs stunts. On the other side, Jager Burton (RG) allowed an 18.2 pressure rate, with an 11.1% pressure rate against the blitz and 20.8% vs stunts. This week, we had Travis Glover (RG) giving up a 3.3% pressure rate, 0% rate against the blitz, 0% against stunts. New Packer Laken Tomlinson gave up a 3.3% pressure rate, 11.1% against the blitz, 0% against stunts. I’m not going to sit here and proclaim that the interior of the line has been fixed, but, against a pretty good Tampa Bay front, Glover and Tomlinson performed well. Defense The Packers lived in Nickel in this game, posting a 90.2% Nickel rate (30.38% above the NFL average). That seems high, until you look and see they were just matching the Bucs’ personnel. The Bucs were in 11 personnel on 90.2% of their snaps. When the Bucs brought out a 3rd WR, the Packers were matching in Nickel. The Packers defense was zone heavy, but not quite as much as they had been. They played Man Coverage on 39.4% of their snaps, their highest rate of the year (their previous high was 13.3% against the Vikings). The Man snaps were primarily Cover 1 (man-to-man across the board, with a single-high safety), but they also ran 2 snaps of Cover 0 (all-out blitz with man coverage). This was also the highest blitz rate the Packers had all year. They blitzed the Bucs on 47.22% of their snaps, 17.09% above NFL average. Their previous high was 34.69% against the Jets. The defense has been a bit uneven at times (which is putting it a bit nicely), but I have been quite happy with Gannon’s blitz approach. Coming into the year, Gannon was known as a defensive coordinator who didn’t blitz very often. This year, he has dialed it up more than we’ve seen in his career, and has leaned heavier into the blitz depending on the gameplan. Seeing that type of flexibility in attack has been really fun. Lukas Van Ness had a nice performance, but not quite as impactful as we had been seeing. He notched 2 solo tackles, 2 assisted tackles and 0 tackles for loss. I’d like to see his pressure rate higher (his 8.7% pressure rate was 3.23% below NFL average), but that was due to a quick release and screen-heavy plan from the Bucs. His Average Time to Pressure was 2.36 seconds, right around NFL average. Albums listened to: Alex G – Camp Miasma Soundtrack; Poppy Ackroyd – Liminal
author: Dusty Evely

title: Green Bay Packers News: Cooper’s injury makes win over Bucs a pyrrhic victory
summary: “We’ve been kind of hit with some type of curse.” Those were Sean Rhyan’s words after the Green Bay Packers’ 17-14 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday afternoon. Yes, the Packers got back in the win column. Yes, the team is back to 2-2 and still right in the thick of the NFC […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 4: Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper #56 of the Green Bay Packers has to be carted off the field in the third quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images “We’ve been kind of hit with some type of curse.” Those were Sean Rhyan’s words after the Green Bay Packers’ 17-14 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday afternoon. Yes, the Packers got back in the win column. Yes, the team is back to 2-2 and still right in the thick of the NFC North race. Yes, the offensive line looked much better, bolstered by changes at both guard positions and facing a team with a fairly dismal pass rush. But when Edgerrin Cooper went down with a non-contact injury in the third quarter, it felt like a massive gut punch for the entire team. Rhyan’s sentiments echo what Packers fans were surely feeling: the likely season-ending loss of yet another essential player on the Green Bay roster. Last year it was Tucker Kraft and Micah Parsons, both of whom were playing at an All-Pro level when they tore their ACLs (and Parsons still managed to be an All-Pro anyway). This year, it has been Jayden Reed and Zach Bako-Bewele, both of whom weren’t quite at that level but who were key cogs on the offense. Now it’s Cooper, who has been pushing for All-Pro consideration as well through the first month of the season. Cooper was even in the midst of arguably his finest game so far this season. Before his injury, he had racked up 9 tackles, a sack, and an interception, the second of his career. It’s probably no coincidence that on the Bucs’ drive immediately following Cooper’s injury, they put together a 12-play, 89-yard touchdown drive to cut the Packers’ lead to three points. Somehow, the defense did just enough to overcome a pair of fourth-quarter turnovers from the Green Bay offense, forcing a punt and a turnover on downs late to preserve a narrow three-point win. But moving forward, the Packers’ defense will be without one of its most dynamic young playmakers, presumably for the rest of the season. Sean Rhyan Nailed It Following Crushing Injury to Packers Star Edgerrin Cooper | SI.com Ryhan isn’t the only Packer who’s feeling down about Cooper’s injury. Isaiah McDuffie, Evan Williams, and Tucker Kraft all spoke about it after the game as well. Rapid reaction: Packers get win, but still ‘hurting ourselves’ | Packers.com Meanwhile, Matt LaFleur wasn’t his usual self at the podium following a win. Quite the opposite: he was fiery and frustrated by the team’s continued mistakes — turnovers and penalties, especially in the fourth quarter, very easily could have led to yet another blown double-digit lead. After a first-quarter interception, he made his way into the backfield three times on the Bucs’ final series, coming up with his first career sack and another QB hit to force a bad throw on the final, decisive fourth down. title: Packers vs. Bears odds: Opening lines for Week 5 matchup
summary: It is particularly unusual for the Green Bay Packers to be underdogs at home in recent years. Since the start of the 2024 season, the Packers have been home underdogs just twice, and one of those games featured the significant unknown of the team starting a backup quarterback. Both of those games came during the […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - DECEMBER 07: Luther Burden III #10 of the Chicago Bears and Carrington Valentine #24 of the Green Bay Packers react after the play during the second quarter at Lambeau Field on December 07, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is particularly unusual for the Green Bay Packers to be underdogs at home in recent years. Since the start of the 2024 season, the Packers have been home underdogs just twice, and one of those games featured the significant unknown of the team starting a backup quarterback. Both of those games came during the 2024 season. Week two saw the Packers — with Malik Willis set to make his first start in relief of an injured Jordan Love — getting 2.5 points against the visiting Indianapolis Colts. Green Bay won that game 16-10, thanks to an efficient 12-for-14 passing day from Willis and 151 rushing yards from Josh Jacobs. The second time that a visiting team was favored at Lambeau Field that year was a few weeks later when the Detroit Lions came to town, and the Lions won 24-14 as 2.5-point favorites. On Sunday in Week 5, the Chicago Bears come to Lambeau likely to feature a backup quarterback, but given the two teams’ recent results, it’s understandable that Chicago is favored at the start of the week. As of Monday morning, FanDuel Sportsbook has the Bears favored by that familiar 2.5-point spread for the two teams’ meeting in the early slate on Sunday. After sitting out the Bears’ prior game against the Eagles with a concussion, backup Tyson Bagent returned in Week 4 and helped lead his team to a 23-12 victory over the New York Jets, throwing for 268 yards and one interception. The Bears completely dominated the game, however, owning the football for nearly 43 minutes of game clock and running a whopping 89 offensive plays to the Jets’ 32. Kyle Monangai was the biggest star for the Chicago offense, toting the football a whopping 30 times for 146 yards and two touchdowns. If the Packers can’t sustain drives on offense and keep their own defense fresh, it could be a very long afternoon next Sunday. Edgerrin Cooper’s absence will likely be a significant blow to the defense as well, particularly with the third-year linebacker having played at an extremely high level to this point in the season. If the Packers offense can find a way to keep Jordan Love clean, there should be opportunities downfield, but the books see only a moderate expectation of offensive firepower; the over/under for total points this week is set at 44.5. title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: Luckily this comes out the next day. My comrade gets to do the day after the day after. He is even luckier. There are some losses that hit harder than others. It is a close game and nail biter in the end. Sometimes the game means more in the standings because of the playoff push. […]
full_text: Luckily this comes out the next day. My comrade gets to do the day after the day after. He is even luckier. There are some losses that hit harder than others. It is a close game and nail biter in the end. Sometimes the game means more in the standings because of the playoff push. Sometimes it is a bitter rival you just don’t want to lose to. Occasionally, all of those intersect into one event that just guts you beyond belief. I will post the numbers and the numbers by themselves tell a great deal of the story, but they are never all of the story. Most of the story is the emotional toll these games take week in and week out. I’d have to look it up, but I don’t think the Texans have ever been 0-4, so at least they are making history. Being a Texans fan is its own special hell. Most 0-4 teams are ready to fold up shop and start playing for next year, but this outfit has had enough miraculous comebacks where you don’t want to fully give up on the season. You can talk yourself into a winning streak. It is the hope that kills you. These numbers by themselves mean little. The Texans have lost in a variety of different ways this season. This isn’t the utter defensive collapse that was 2010. It isn’t the pick six festival that was 2013. It hasn’t been any one thing and that is the most maddening part of it. The only consistent thing has been an inability to make the one or two key plays that winning reams make. Three of the four losses were one score games. We might as well call them the “Almost” Texans. The Key Numbers Total Yards: Texans 52/397, Cowboys 73/399 Rushing Yards: Texans 19/62, Cowboys 25/75 Passing Yards: Texans 33/335, Cowboys 48/324 Third Down Conversions: Texans 3/10, Cowboys 5/14 Fourth Down Conversions: Texans 0/0, Cowboys 1/1 Sacks: Texans 3, Cowboys 2 Turnovers: Texans 0, Cowboys 0 Penalties: Texans 13/90, Cowboys 6/47 Time of Possession: Texans 28:33, Cowboys 31:27 These numbers tell a story, but it might not be the story of the game. The stories are usually when these things happen. For instance, two sacks is not terrible. I’m sure Nick Caley would gladly take only two sacks allowed per game for the rest of the season. Unfortunately, it is about when these sacks happened. They happened at a stage in the game when they desperately needed sustained drives and instead they were three and outs. However, that spills us into the good, bad, and ugly. The Good We will get to Stroud in his own special section, so this one goes to Will Anderson yet again. Officially he had only a half a sack and five tackles but a couple of those were tackles for loss. As the Texans ponder their future they will need building blocks. These seasons reveal a ton about character. There are players that consider it a night at the office and make business decisions in key moments. Then there are players like Anderson. J.D. Clowney also had half a sack in his return to the field. Whatever is happening on defense, it is not happening on the defensive line. Throw in Danielle Hunter and you have a group of players getting constant pressure on Dak Prescott. Unfortunately, the units behind the defensive line didn’t play as well, but we as fans notice the players that show up and play hard and they will always be called out for their effort. The Bad I cannot completely torch Nick Caley for this effort. Any time you score 30 points and you don’t turn the football over it is a good day. However, there are still key points in these games when protections break down and play calls don’t make sense. More than anything, I hate days like today. They are the days that get stat heads like me (yup, I’ll cop to this one) to say that things are going well overall because they scored a ton of points in two games. The most important thing is that the Cowboys were yet another weak defensive team that struggles against the run. Yet, they looked like the 1985 Bears against the run. The Texans rushed for more than 100 yards in the first game and haven’t sniffed that since. For a hard-nosed physical football team that is pretty anemic. The offense deserves their portion of the blame for the defensive debacle. They couldn’t posses the ball long enough to keep the Cowboys offense off the field. You cannot let them run 70+ plays and live to tell about it. The Cowboys ran 20 more plays than the Texans and that is a recipe for disaster. The Ugly Someone needs to explain this to me like I’m a four year old. How do you allow a player to catch 17 passes in a football game? Yes, I know that Kamari Lassiter should have been a Pro Bowler and Derek Stingley was a Pro Bowler. The operative word there is was. They aren’t playing like that now for whatever reason. They aren’t bad football players per se. They still make plays and do good things, but they are not playing on the level they were last season. At a certain point you have to scrap what you are doing and do something else. The drive that pulled the Cowboys within 23-20 was the key drive of the game. The Texans stopped them twice inside the ten only to have penalties extend the drive. The first defensive holding/contact penalty on Lassiter was EXTREMELY questionable. George Pickens initiated most of the contact, so it was a horrible flag. The second penalty was not egregious. The Texans literally turned them over on downs after another set of downs where the Cowboys were ready to settle for a field goal. That was eight plays inside the ten. Even the Texans could score a touchdown in those conditions. That segment probably was the whole football game. It also encapsulates the season as a whole. Focus on Stroud I’ll have more to say on this later in the week, but the Texans have some huge decisions looming and none are bigger than the decision on Stroud. Yet, today was the first day I honestly considered Stroud’s point of view. Does he really want to be here? If he keeps ballin’ like he has the first four weeks the answer could be no. No, he is not going to make anyone forget Peyton Manning, Drew Brees, or Tom Brady, but he has mustered five touchdown passes in four games and thrown zero picks. He is one of three quarterbacks not to throw one. I could nitpick in this one, but what would be the point? Stroud threw for nearly 350 yards without a run game. He needed a drive at the end of the game and gave his team a lead with two minutes left. I’m not sure what else anyone wants from him. I will own up to my part in this whole thing. I questioned his abilities coming into the season saying that he is not an elite quarterback. I still don’t know that he is, but this 0-4 start is not on him. He is doing what they are asking him to do. That of course brings up the next obvious question. Are they using him to his most effective use? The answer is almost clearly no. We will have more on this later in the week as the whispers at 0-2 and 0-3 become raised voices at 0-4. They will become shouting and screaming with future losses. There is no joy in Mudville. The Texans are strung out.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: ESPN’s Adam Schefter alludes to Colts, among suitors, who have called on Marvin Harrison Jr. regarding trade availability
summary: According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter on ‘The Pat McAfee Show,’ the Indianapolis Colts are among the league suitors who have already called the Arizona Cardinals on the trade availability of underperforming young wideout Marvin Harrison Jr. ahead of the NFL’s upcoming Tuesday, November 10th trade deadline: Originally the 4th overall pick of the 2024 NFL […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - SEPTEMBER 27: Marvin Harrison Jr. #18 of the Arizona Cardinals heads to the locker room before an NFL game against the San Francisco 49ers on September 27, 2026 at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter on ‘The Pat McAfee Show,’ the Indianapolis Colts are among the league suitors who have already called the Arizona Cardinals on the trade availability of underperforming young wideout Marvin Harrison Jr. ahead of the NFL’s upcoming Tuesday, November 10th trade deadline: Who's calling about Marvin Harrison Jr… The Indianapolis Colts are calling #PMSLive https://t.co/Ogpi7ipwdA pic.twitter.com/QBTdCDdb3x — Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) October 5, 2026 Originally the 4th overall pick of the 2024 NFL Draft by Arizona, and widely considered a “can’t miss,” if not a generational wideout prospect, the 24-year-old wideout has largely (and surprisingly) struggled in over 2 seasons with the Cardinals—having been an increasing afterthought within their offense compared to their other starting receivers. Of course, he’s also the namesake of his legendary father, Marvin Harrison Sr., who’s a Pro Football Hall of Famer and the all-time greatest wide receiver in Indianapolis franchise history, as the leader in nearly all of their major statistical receiving categories. However, Jr.‘s much bigger than his famous pops, at 6,‘3”, 220 pounds, but otherwise, it’s not hard to miss the uncanny physical resemblance between the two wideouts. There’s been unnamed speculation that Harrison’s Jr. trade value has fallen to a ‘quality Day 3 pick,’ as in some anonymous league circles, he’s viewed more as a “3rd wide receiver with upside.” That being said, it’s hard to envision the Cardinals actually moving him elsewhere, unless they get meaningful trade value in return, in some ways, similarly to the Colts have handled backup quarterback Anthony Richardson’s availability to-date. For what it’s worth, Harrison Jr. just had his first touchdown reception of the season in Week 4, but otherwise, has underwhelmed to just 5 receptions for 85 total receiving yards collectively through Arizona’s first four games. It seems like a combination of maturity, underperformance, and not being properly utilized by the Arizona offense. While I won’t get too into the weeds again of why Harrison Jr. makes sense for the Colts , it’s clear that after losing lead wideout Alec Pierce to injured reserve and veteran Keenan Allen now banged up, having missed last weekend’s game, that Indianapolis could use some immediate positional reinforcements, especially with veteran pickup Darius Slayton still not active through two weeks of being with the team. Harrison Jr. would be a legacy here, and the hope is that Colts wide receivers coach Reggie Wayne, who formed one of the most prolific wide receiver duos in NFL history alongside Harrison Jr.‘s father, could coach some “tough love” into the still young and talented wideout, who may just need a change of scenery to reach his full playing career potential. If nothing else, it seems like a fairly favorable ‘buy-low’ opportunity for a former top wideout prospect, who almost every team coveted not too long ago ahead of the 2024 NFL Draft— with the Colts being among them .
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Colts’ performances from Week 4 win across the pond
summary: After an initial sloppy start, the Indianapolis Colts (2-2) righted the trolleybus offensively, took advantage of a rookie 3rd-string quarterback defensively, and bested the Washington Commanders (1-3), 30-13, in London this past Sunday—now back to playing .500 football for the first time this season. We’ll look at some of the studs, duds, and maybe a […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Tottenham, ENG; Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner (99) hits Washington Commanders quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis (16) during the second quarter at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Geoff Burke-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect After an initial sloppy start, the Indianapolis Colts (2-2) righted the trolleybus offensively, took advantage of a rookie 3rd-string quarterback defensively, and bested the Washington Commanders (1-3), 30-13, in London this past Sunday—now back to playing .500 football for the first time this season. We’ll look at some of the studs, duds, and maybe a little in between regarding their latest international win: Horsepower RB Jonathan Taylor: The Colts star workhorse continues to shine overseas, recording 95 total rushing yards and 2 rushing touchdowns on 20 carries (4.8 ypc. avg.). With starting quarterback Daniel Jones clearly shaky play early on (which we’ll get to here in a bit), the Colts went “back to the basics,” and that was riding the efficient Taylor in this one (with some rookie rusher Seth McGowan sprinkled in as a change-of-pace back). Taylor is now the all-time international leading rusher (6 touchdowns) and rushing yards leader (408) in league history, and whether it was “drinking tea” or “waving like the queen” following his two touchdowns runs on the day, he celebrated in London style. DT DeForest Buckner: With the Colts offense spiraling early on (with a fumble lost, three straight punts, and an interception on their first five offensive drives), Buckner, to me, almost single-handedly kept the Colts in this football game defensively with his hustle, impact, and leadership. Whether it was stopping the run, creating pass pressure, or just all-out effort , Buckner played like a man on a mission, and was a huge reason why the Indianapolis defense held the Commanders to just two field goals on their first two offensive drives, despite being gifted a short field on their first possession because of the weird Jones’ fumble. Buckner deserves to be a Colts’ Ring of Honor player when it’s all said-and-done, and his collective impact on Sunday is a big reason why. That was a performance to remember, one day looking back at his standout career here in Indianapolis. While we’re on the position, I’d also like to give backup defensive tackle Ade Adebawore an honorable mention, who made his pass rushing presence felt in limited action again, with 0.5 sacks and 2 QB hits. He continues to be a menace as a subpackage interior pass rusher. LB Jaylon Carlies: The Colts much maligned starting linebacker unit has taken its fair share of lumps and growing criticism to begin the 2026 campaign, but arguably had their best performance of the season on Sunday. In particular, Carlies showcased his best, and elite athleticism, by somehow batting an Athan Kaliakmanis pass to himself for the interception early in the 3rd quarter . CB Charvarius Ward : The Colts secondary had its fair share of coverage gaffes, by allowing a handful of explosive big plays to the rookie Kaliakmanis, but wearing the guardians cap again, Ward arguably had his best game of the season in coverage. Specifically, he allowed just two receptions for 13 total receiving yards on 7 targets in coverage (28.6 catch rate) with 3 pass breakups . PK Spencer Shrader: Regarding what was a narrowly won offseason competition, the Colts absolutely made the right call by naming Shrader the victor, who was a perfect 3 for 3 from field goal range again including makes from 48 yards, 52 yards, and 44 yards. That’ll certainly play on special teams! Horseplay QB Daniel Jones : For the first 1.5 quarters in this one, Jones looked like how a lot of Colts fans may have thought he’d look coming off last year’s season-ending torn Achilles in Week 14 with no preseason reps. He has to take better care of the football on the weird sack fumble, and the interception off his back-foot under duress to Commanders veteran cornerback Rasul Douglas is just a play that can’t happen at this level. Jones has to either feel the pressure earlier or “eat the sack,” rather than throw a gifted lollipop in coverage. Jones looked closer to the failed franchise quarterback hopeful who was too turnover prone with the New York Giants than the breakout quarterback we surprisingly saw during the first half of last season in his Indianapolis debut. No idea if the Colts coaching staff was ever seriously contemplating an in-game change, but one more offensive drive that ended in another Jones brutal turnover, and as fans, we were realistically getting close to advocating for seeing Anthony Richardson again—if we weren’t already. Jones absolutely cannot play that way again in Pittsburgh next week, which has been a historical franchise house of horrors. CB Sauce Gardner: Whether you want to argue that Gardner has not lived up to his billing so far in Indianapolis, after the Colts surprisingly surrendered two first round picks, it’s fair game—although Gardner himself did not make that trade. In London, he clearly played his worst game as a member of the Colts. He allowed 4 receptions for 117 total receiving yards and a touchdown reception on his 5 pass coverage targets , although I will also contend that his safety help (i.e., rookie A.J. Haulcy) and the Indy pass pressure didn’t do him favors either by leaving him on a coverage island for so long. Even with his lack of interceptions, the Colts need Gardner to be a shutdown #1 cornerback, and on Sunday, he was far from it, as he was openly picked on by Kaliakmanis on two explosive passing plays deep.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Colts Monday Morning Awards: Week 4 vs Commanders (London)
summary: The Colts shook off an ugly first quarter and leaned on their run game to walk out of Tottenham Hotspur Stadium with a convincing 30-13 win over the Washington Commanders. Was the first month of the season pretty? Absolutely not, but the Stampede Blue Community would have accepted a 2-2 record after a tough stretch […]
full_text: London, United Kingdom - October 4: Robert Henry Jr. of Washington Commanders is tackled by Indianapolis Colts linebacker Jaylon Carlies during the Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders match at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 4, 2026 in London, United Kingdom. (Photo by Vince Mignott/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images) | DeFodi Images via Getty Images The Colts shook off an ugly first quarter and leaned on their run game to walk out of Tottenham Hotspur Stadium with a convincing 30-13 win over the Washington Commanders. Was the first month of the season pretty? Absolutely not, but the Stampede Blue Community would have accepted a 2-2 record after a tough stretch against the Ravens, Chiefs, Texans and Commanders, in that order. The defense stepped up and dominated third down, while the rushing attack took over and Jonathan Taylor continued cementing his name into the NFL record books as an international superstar. Here’s to a new edition of Monday Morning Awards. MVP of the Game: Jonathan Taylor Who else deserves it other than the best player on the roster? Taylor rushed for 95 yards and two touchdowns on 20 carries, becoming both the NFL’s all-time leading rusher and scorer in international games. After he bounced left for a 5-yard score to give the Colts a lead they would never relinquish, he celebrated his fifth touchdown of the season by sitting criss-cross applesauce to veritably sip tea in front of a roaring crowd in London. TAYLOR TOUCHDOWN #INDsWAS on NFLN pic.twitter.com/p1WfMtYoA4 — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 4, 2026 With 75 career touchdowns, Indy’s 27-year-old tailback joined Jim Brown, Emmitt Smith, and LaDainian Tomlinson as the only running backs to reach that mark before turning 28. Taylor doesn’t turn 28 until after the regular season and wild card weekend ends. Dud of the Game: Daniel Jones performance The dud of the game came from Daniel Jones, who was strip-sacked by Odafe Oweh and lost the fumble, giving Washington possession near the Colts’ red zone on the second snap from scrimmage. Jones later threw an interception off his back foot to cornerback Rasul Douglas, marking his eighth turnover-worthy play through four games and putting the Colts in an early deficit before he finally settled in. The veteran QB finished 19 of 34 for just 143 passing yards, but scrambled for a 4-yard touchdown to put the Colts ahead by two scores early in the fourth quarter. Daniel Jones!!! #INDvsWAS on NFLN pic.twitter.com/5AYd8dcQVP — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 4, 2026 Worst Play of the Game: Turnover terminates opening drive The worst play of the game has to be the opening sequence as the Colts had the ball for just two snaps before Jones fumbled and gave Washington a chance to seize an early lead on a short field. Oweh rushed from the right edge and drove left tackle Bernhard Raimann straight into Jones’ dropback, which knocked the ball loose before Oweh recovered it himself. Best Play of the Game: Jaylon Carlies interception If the first half was hard to stomach, any doubt of leaving London without a victory vanished when the defense finally got the momentum-shifting turnover it needed to start the third quarter. Washington was pushed backward from a penalty and faced with third-and-17, then linebacker Jaylon Carlies reached up to tip a pass from opposing QB Athan Kaliakmanis, hauled in his first career interception and returned it inside the red zone. Four plays later, Taylor plunged into the end zone to give Indianapolis a 17-6 lead. Heck of a play from @Colts LB Jaylon Carlies @INDvsWAS on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/am18AmEMmD — NFL (@NFL) October 4, 2026 Best Position Group: Defensive line The defensive front combined for 14 stops and 11 QB hits, then made life miserable as the Commanders were able to convert just 2-of-15 third downs. Laiatu Latu and Adetomiwa Adebawore combined for a sack that knocked opposing starter Marcus Mariota out of the game, while Latu added two more quarterback hits. DeForest Buckner had three quarterback hits of his own, and collected his 100th career tackle for loss. The biggest difference was the pressure as Washington could not move the sticks with its emergency third-string QB. Unsung Hero: Spencer Shrader Kicker Spencer Shrader made all three field goals from 48, 52, and 44-yards out to keep the Colts ahead with enough cushion to maintain a lead. His 52-yarder in the third quarter pushed the Colts’ lead back to seven after Washington had trimmed the deficit to 17-13. Shrader quietly put together one of those games where you don’t notice the kicker until you look at the scoreboard and realize he has as many points as the opponent. Along with three extra points, Shrader collected 12 points while the Commanders left 13 on the scoreboard. Rookie of the Week: Seth McGowan Rookie running back Seth McGowan didn’t need a huge workload, but his 10 touches were more than enough to make an impact. With Taylor doing most of the heavy-lifting, McGowan carried the ball six times for 31 yards, averaging 5.2 per carry. Two of those six carries resulted in first downs as the seventh-rounder provided a nice change of pace and showed why he’s capable of getting more opportunities. McGowan also returned four kickoffs for 102 total return yards, with the final return ultimately shifting the Commanders’ momentum and led to a field goal. Honorable Mention: Walley Ward Sunday was Justin Walley’s best game of his young career. He finished with eight tackles and a key sack on an blitz that forced a fourth down and knocked the Commanders out of field-goal range. Walley came screaming uncovered from the blindside and dropped Kaliakmanis for a 9-yard sack that forced Washington to punt. Walley posted a 75.4 coverage grade, which ranked among the top 10 cornerbacks who played at least 10 coverage snaps in Week 4. Watch out for Walley 👀 #INDvsWAS on NFLN pic.twitter.com/ymbykBpdUA — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 4, 2026 Charvarius Ward deserves credit when its due, too. Washington completed only two catches against him on seven targets, while Ward recorded three forced incompletions. His three forced incompletions and 41 snaps per reception were third among cornerbacks through Sunday in Week 4. Indy struggled to start the game, but played complementary football in the second half. The Colts finished with just one penalty compared to Washington’s 10 and won the turnover battle after the early mistake. Between the clean play, dominance on third down and pounding the rock with their marquee tailback, the Colts stuck to their playstyle and return stateside with an even 2-2 record. The Colts travel to Pittsburgh to face the Steelers (2-2) next Sunday, with kickoff set for 1 p.m.
author: Thomas Butler-Guerrero

title: The Colts won, but Daniel Jones needs to get a grip
summary: The Indianapolis Colts found some much-needed fortune in London as they managed to beat the Washington Commanders and climb to 2-2. Yes, there was skill and preparation involved, but there was a lot of luck as well. Daniel Jones tested that luck throughout the game, but if the Colts are going to keep winning, they […]
full_text: London, United Kingdom - October 4: Tim Settle of Washington Commanders and Daniel Jones of Indianapolis Colts battle for the ball during the Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders match between Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 4, 2026 in London, United Kingdom. (Photo by Vince Mignott/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images) | DeFodi Images via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts found some much-needed fortune in London as they managed to beat the Washington Commanders and climb to 2-2. Yes, there was skill and preparation involved, but there was a lot of luck as well. Daniel Jones tested that luck throughout the game, but if the Colts are going to keep winning, they need to reserve some in the tank. The best way to do that is for Jones to stop turning the ball over. Jones fumbled on the second play of the game in a highly unusual fashion. It wasn’t as bizarre as the “butt fumble”, but it looked just as sloppy. The defender bull rushed Bernhard Raimann and had them both in Jones’ face, but to fumble the ball like that was simply odd. Just like against the Texans, he threw off his back foot under pressure and was intercepted. It was a dispiriting quarter and a half as the offense was dreadful. Luckily, the Colts weathered the early storm. The defense held strong and kept the Commanders out of the endzone to limit the damage to six. Additionally, facing a third string quarterback didn’t hurt either. That isn’t always going to be the case, however. The better teams in this league will make the Colts pay for their errors. Jones has to be better. He has to protect the ball and play smarter. He cannot turn the ball over at this rate if the Colts hope to survive. Daniel Jones has seven turnovers across four games with five in the last two. That looks like the second half of 2025 Jones, but the Colts can’t win with that version. An occasional turnover is understandable, but at least two of the fumbles and both of the interceptions were avoidable. Those must be cleaned up. Jones has to find a way to get a grip.

title: Colts-Steelers opening odds:  Steal one in the Steel City
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are heading to a dark place. Game day may be bright and sunny with the perfect temperature and the right amount of wind, but it is sure to send a chill down the spine of Colts Nation. Facing the Pittsburgh Steelers in Pittsburgh has almost never gone well, but the Colts get […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 27: A detailed view of aPittsburgh Steelers helmet on the field prior to an NFL football game between the Cincinnati Bengals and Pittsburgh Steelers on September 27, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are heading to a dark place. Game day may be bright and sunny with the perfect temperature and the right amount of wind, but it is sure to send a chill down the spine of Colts Nation. Facing the Pittsburgh Steelers in Pittsburgh has almost never gone well, but the Colts get a chance to right some wrongs next week. FanDuel Sportsbook has the Colts as underdogs at +1.5 points in the spread. The money line starts at +112 while the over/under comes in at 41.5. The Colts have gotten their season back on track after an 0-2 start. Wins against the Texans and Commanders have them pointed in the right direction. Concerning play from Daniel Jones continues to be a mild theme as turnovers and a lack of positive ball movement were the story for the offense in the first half. Luckily, Jonathan Taylor wears a horseshoe, and the defense kept this one close enough for the Colts to pull comfortably ahead and reach .500. The Steelers found themselves on the rare side of an “L” to the Cleveland Browns. It’s a rivalry that’s actually become more of a true division battle over the years than it used to be, though. The old Browns would have rolled over after falling behind 0-7 to start, but this is the 3-1 Browns. They scored the next 21 and held the Steelers off with a late-game field goal. The Steelers will be looking to get that taste out of their mouths. This is a huge game for the Colts. A 2-3 to start the year with their schedule is something most fans would have taken. Now that they are at 2-2, however, 3-2 sounds much better. It will be a chance to continue their streak and build contender status in the league by picking up a solid win against an opponent that causes them fits. This could mark a major season shift.

title: 3 Numbers to Know From the Jaguars’ Win Over the Bengals
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars eeked out a win over the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 4 to move to 3-1 on the season. Hooray! Here are a few stats that stand out from the victory. 125 That’s how many yards the Jaguars were penalized on Sunday. It’s the most by Jacksonville since Week 7 of the 2019 […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - OCTOBER 4: Ventrell Miller #51 of the Jacksonville Jaguars celebrates during the third quarter of a game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars eeked out a win over the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 4 to move to 3-1 on the season. Hooray! Here are a few stats that stand out from the victory. 125 That’s how many yards the Jaguars were penalized on Sunday. It’s the most by Jacksonville since Week 7 of the 2019 season… when the Jags beat the Bengals in Cincinnati, 27-17. Head coach Liam Coen said after the game, “I’ve never been a part of anything like that before in my life.” Liam Coen didn’t want to get fined commenting about penalties in the first half 🤣 “I’m not going to say anything to get fined. That was just mental. I’ve just never seen something quite that much in the first half of a football game.” #Jaguars #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/MgJVds9JyW — Action Sports Jax (@ActionSportsJax) October 4, 2026 The Jaguars had 10 penalties for 125 yards, and the Bengals weren’t far behind (11 for 108). And the teams really weren’t that sloppy. Sure, there were a few obvious calls, but most of the flags should’ve been picked up. Or not called in the first place. Jacksonville had two touchdowns, an interception, and a lengthy kickoff return nullified by penalties. They still found a way to get the job done. Though they may not have beaten the “can’t stop great passers” allegations, they did quiet the “can’t finish ball games” concerns. 23 That’s how many rushing yards the Jaguars allowed on Sunday. It’s the fifth-fewest in franchise history. Fewest single-game rushing yards allowed by #Jaguars in franchise history (regular season/playoffs) … 10 by KC (Oct. 2007) 14 by Arizona (Nov. 2013) 14 by Detroit (Nov. 2016) 21 by MIami (Jan. 2000) 23 by Cincinnati … today Per @pfref — Ryan O'Halloran (@ryanohalloran) October 4, 2026 Jacksonville has now gone 21 straight games without allowing a single rusher to reach 75 yards on the ground. That’s the fourth-longest streak by any team in the Super Bowl era, per ESPN . Bengals starter Chase Brown couldn’t get anything going — he finished with 10 rushing yards on 9 carries. Joe Burrow and Samaje Perine chipped in 6 and 7 yards, respectively, on 3 carries apiece. That adds up to 1.5 yards per rush for Cincinnati. Burrow may have thrown for 428 yards, but he wasn’t all that efficient. The Jaguars held him to 7.9 yards per attempt. He had more interceptions (2) than touchdowns (1). By completely shutting down the run, Jacksonville forced Cincinnati to be one-dimensional on offense. Burrow couldn’t get the job done. 3:1 That’s the ratio of how often Jarrian Jones was targeted in coverage compared to Travis Hunter on Sunday. Hunter was targeted 6 times, per PFF. He allowed 3 catches for 20 yards while notching 2 pass breakups. Jones was targeted EIGHTEEN TIMES, allowing 11 catches for 133 yards. He had 1 pass breakup. Jones finished with a 59.6 coverage grade, which seems about right, but there should probably be a grading curve. The guy was going against some elite receivers in Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. After Chase left the game in the first half with a concussion, Higgins became the focal point of Cincinnati’s offense, and Jones matched up against him for much of the game. Half of Jones’ targets in coverage went to Higgins. He finished with 4 catches for 56 yards against Jones, compared to 7 catches for 101 yards against all other Jaguars defenders. It was far from Jones’ best game — but it’s not like he was burned over and over again. He did just enough to help Jacksonville pull out a road victory against a playoff contender. He didn’t come close to acing the test, but in my book, he passed it. For context, JJ was playing boundary CB all day. He was primarily aligned over Tee Higgins since he is the Bengals’ X receiver. With Chase leaving the game early, more targets went to Higgins. Also, the Jags played a lot of Cover 2 and Cover 6 (1/4, 1/4 and 1/2) wirh JJ playing… https://t.co/sVJKr2Jn0h — Bucky Brooks (@BuckyBrooks) October 5, 2026 Hunter had an easier assignment than Jones, but man oh man, he passed this week’s test with flying colors. He had a teach tape PBU , a leaping PBU , a colossal tackle , and a filthy interception negated by a penalty. The Heisman Trophy winner earned an 80.8 coverage grade from PFF. Other numbers to know: 9 . That’s how many consecutive games the Jaguars have with an interception. It’s the longest streak in franchise history and the longest active streak in the NFL. 38 . That’s how many points off takeaways the Jaguars have this season. It’s the most in the NFL. 3 . That’s how many redzone takeaways the Jaguars have this season. No other team has more than 1. 0 . That’s how many first half touchdowns the Jaguars have allowed this season. They’re the first team to do so in each of their first four games since the 2022 49ers. 95 . That’s how many receiving yards Brenton Strange had on Sunday. It is a new career-high for him. 25 . That’s how long Chris Rodriguez’s rushing touchdown was on Sunday. It is a new career-high for him. 100% . That’s how often Travis Hunter was on the field for Jacksonville’s defensive snaps on Sunday. It is a new career-high for him. 0% . That’s how often Travis Hunter was on the field for Jacksonville’s offensive snaps on Sunday. It is a new career-low for him. 55 . That’s how many consecutive games Jakobi Meyers has had a 1st down catch. It’s the longest active streak in the NFL. 81 .
